item.title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, that leads to such great benefit as heedfulness. Heedfulness, monks, leads to great benefit.”
item.description:
“I do not see any other thing, monks, that leads to such great benefit as heedfulness. Heedfulness, monks, leads to great benefit.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.83
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Form, monks, is suffering. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of form — that too is suffering. Form that has arisen from suffering, monks,…
item.description:
“Form, monks, is suffering. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of form — that too is suffering. Form that has arisen from suffering, monks, how could it be happiness? Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is suffering. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of consciousness — that too is suffering. Consciousness that has arisen from suffering, monks, how could it be happiness? Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … disenchanted with feeling … disenchanted with perception … disenchanted with formations … disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate … He knows: ‘… there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.19
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Poṭṭhapāda, when defiling states are eliminated, pure states increase; here and now, by direct knowledge, one realizes and abides in fully developed, vast wisdom. Then…
item.description:
“Poṭṭhapāda, when defiling states are eliminated, pure states increase; here and now, by direct knowledge, one realizes and abides in fully developed, vast wisdom. Then joy arises, gladness, tranquility, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and a pleasant abiding arise.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 9 – Poṭṭhapādasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Thus, great king, a monk contemplates the five hindrances not yet abandoned as a debt, as a disease, as a prison, as slavery, as a…
item.description:
“Thus, great king, a monk contemplates the five hindrances not yet abandoned as a debt, as a disease, as a prison, as slavery, as a desert road. And, great king, just as being without debt, without disease, freed from prison, freed from slavery, in a safe and pleasant land — so, great king, a monk contemplates the five hindrances when they have been abandoned.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 2 – Sāmaññaphalasutta

item.title: Elder Māṇava: “I saw an old person, I saw a sick person in pain, I saw a dead person, With life exhausted — Therefore I…
item.description:
Elder Māṇava:
“I saw an old person,
I saw a sick person in pain,
I saw a dead person,
With life exhausted —
Therefore I went forth,
Leaving the home life,
Abandoning sensual pleasures
That are enticing and agreeable.”

From: Theragāthā 1.73

item.title: “Therefore, Māgandiya, associate with true persons. By associating with true persons, you will hear the true Dhamma. By hearing the true Dhamma, you will live…
item.description:
“Therefore, Māgandiya, associate with true persons. By associating with true persons, you will hear the true Dhamma. By hearing the true Dhamma, you will live in accordance with the Dhamma and the proper Dhamma. By living in accordance with the Dhamma and the proper Dhamma, you will know and see for yourself: ‘These are diseases, boils, darts. Here, these diseases, boils, darts are abandoned without remainder. Because clinging ceases in me, becoming ceases; because becoming ceases, birth ceases; because birth ceases, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 75 – Māgandiyasutta

item.title: … Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One: Life is swept along, Short is the lifespan…
item.description:
… Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
Life is swept along,
Short is the lifespan —
To old age we are led,
There is no stopping place.
Seeing this danger in death,
Do meritorious deeds
That bring true happiness.

(The Blessed One):
Life is swept along,
Short is the lifespan —
To old age we are led,
There is no stopping place.
Seeing this danger in death,
Seeking peace, abandon worldly hopes.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.3
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Contact, monks, is one extreme. The origination of contact is the second extreme. The cessation of contact is the middle. Craving is the weaver; for…
item.description:
“Contact, monks, is one extreme. The origination of contact is the second extreme. The cessation of contact is the middle. Craving is the weaver; for craving weaves one to be reborn in this or that state of existence. Thus, monks, a monk directly knows what should be directly known, fully understands what should be fully understood. By directly knowing what should be directly known and fully understanding what should be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering here and now.
Knowing both extremes,
Not stained in the middle,
I call that great person,
He has surpassed the weaver.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.61
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye — desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing; sounds cognizable…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye — desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear … odors … tastes … touches cognizable by the body — desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. Although they are not sensual pleasures, monks, in the noble one’s discipline they are called the strands of sensual pleasure.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.63

item.title: One whose mind is like a rock, Firm, not shaken, Without greed for the agreeable, Without hatred for the disagreeable — One whose mind is…
item.description:
One whose mind is like a rock,
Firm, not shaken,
Without greed for the agreeable,
Without hatred for the disagreeable —
One whose mind is thus developed —
From where can suffering come?

From: Udana 4.4
